lines.translit: Gilgāmeš ana šâšu-ma izakkara ana Ūta-napišti rūqi

i18n.en: Gilgamesh spoke to him — to Utnapishtim the Distant:

lines.commentary: Utnapishtim's standing-epithet *rūqu* — 'distant, far-away' — is preserved here as 'the Distant' (Foster 2005). George 2003 renders 'the Faraway'; Kovacs 'the Far-Distant'. The Akkadian carries both spatial-cosmographic and temporal-archaic connotations (Utnapishtim dwells at *pī nārāti*, the mouth-of-the-rivers cosmic-periphery — XI:197). The cross-corpus flood-survivor-name cluster Ziusudra / Atra-ḫasīs / Utnapishtim / Noach is treated at the central entry `ziusudra-atrahasis-utnapishtim-noach-flood-survivor-name-cluster-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: "I gaze upon you, Utnapishtim —

lines.translit: minâtu-ka ul šanâ kī yâši-ma atta

i18n.en: your features are no different — you are just like me.

lines.translit: u atta ul šanâta kī yâši-ma atta

i18n.en: And you yourself are not different — just like me you are.
My heart was wholly set to do battle (with you),
but [you] sit at your ease — idle.

lines.translit: qibâ yâši kī tazziz-ma ina puḫur ilāni balāṭa teššēʾi

i18n.en: Tell me — how is it that you stood in the assembly of the gods and obtained (eternal) life?"

lines.commentary: *balāṭu* — the Akkadian noun for 'life, vitality, continued-existence' (CAD B 46-63) — carries the technical sense of *immortality* here, paralleling the *napišta dāriti* 'eternal life' formula of Adapa A:10. The parenthetical '(eternal)' surfaces the technical-sense without losing the literal Akkadian. Gilgamesh's question frames the entire flood-narrative as Utnapishtim's testimony to the *how* of his deification — the cross-corpus structural-inversion with Adapa's *lost-immortality* is documented at the central entry `utnapishtim-deification-vs-adapa-immortality-loss-cross-corpus`.

lines.translit: Ūta-napišti ana šâšu-ma izakkara ana Gilgāmeš

i18n.en: Utnapishtim spoke to him — to Gilgamesh:
"Let me reveal to you, Gilgamesh, a hidden matter,

lines.commentary: The proem of the flood-narrative. *amāt niṣirti* — 'word of the hidden/secret matter' — the same phrase recurs at XI:268 where Utnapishtim is about to reveal the plant-of-rejuvenation. The two *amāt niṣirti* moments frame the entire Gilgamesh-XI encounter as the *transmission of two hidden things* from Utnapishtim to Gilgamesh: the flood-story (XI:9-203) and the plant (XI:268-285). The framework is wisdom-revelation, paralleling Ea's *piriš-ti ilāni* 'secret of the gods' (XI:10).

i18n.en: and the secret of the gods let me tell you.
Shuruppak — the city that you yourself know,

lines.commentary: Shuruppak (modern Tell Fara) is one of the five Sumerian antediluvian cities (see existing central entry `five-antediluvian-cities-eridug-bad-tibira-larag-zimbir-shuruppag-cross-corpus`); it is the home-city of Ziusudra in the Sumerian Flood Story tradition. Cross-corpus: the Sumerian King List names Ubar-Tutu of Shuruppak as the last antediluvian king (XI:23 names Utnapishtim as *son of Ubar-Tutu*, identifying him with the Ziusudra-line). The Hebrew tradition has no city-of-Noah; the rupture-and-rebuilding-from-scratch model.

lines.translit: ālu ša ina kišād Purattim šaknu

i18n.en: the city that lies on the bank of the Euphrates —
that city was already ancient, and the gods (dwelt) within it,

lines.translit: ana šakāni a-bu-bi ub-lu libbi-šunu ilānu rabûtu

i18n.en: when the great gods' hearts were moved to bring on a flood.

lines.commentary: The Akkadian idiom *abālu* G ('to carry, bring') with *libbu* ('heart') as subject — *the heart drove (them) to* — frames the flood-decision as collective divine-deliberation. Cross-corpus to Atrahasis II.viii (the noise-rationale); Gen 6:5-7 (YHWH's wickedness-rationale); Qur'an 11:25-49 (the prophet-rejection rationale) — four traditions, one fixed narrative-slot, four distinct causation-rationales. Documented at the new central entry `flood-causation-divine-council-gilgamesh-atrahasis-genesis-qur-an-cross-corpus`. Notable: the Gilgamesh-XI tradition leaves the *cause* of the divine-decision unstated; the cause is left as divine-prerogative-without-justification.

i18n.en: Their father Anu bound them by oath,
their counsellor — the warrior Enlil,
their throne-bearer Ninurta,
their canal-inspector Ennugi —
Prince Ea was with them, bound by the (same) oath.
Their word he repeated to the reed-hut:

lines.commentary: The reed-wall warning is Ea's technical solution to the bound-by-oath problem: Ea cannot directly warn Utnapishtim (he is bound by the divine-council oath at XI:15-19), but he can address the reed-hut wall in Utnapishtim's hearing. The trope is the diagnostic Mesopotamian Ea-warning device, treated at the existing central entry `iz-zi-da-kikkish-talking-through-the-wall-to-keep-an-oath-flood-trope-cross-corpus`. The Ea-warning-deception-misadvice-test crux (whether Ea is honestly warning, deceitfully misadvising, or strategically testing) is treated at the central entry `ea-warning-deception-misadvice-test-crux-cross-corpus` — extended in this editor pass to include the Gilgamesh-XI Ea-warning refIds.

i18n.en: "Reed-hut, reed-hut! Wall, wall!
Reed-hut, hearken! Wall, pay heed!
Man of Shuruppak, son of Ubar-Tutu!
Demolish your house — build a boat!

lines.commentary: The boat-build command opens the construction-section (XI:24-78). The Akkadian *eleppu* — Sumerian-loanword from *e-lep* — is the standard Akkadian flood-vessel term, paralleled by Sumerian *ma2 gur4-gur4* (Flood Story D:5) and Hebrew *tevah* (Gen 6:14). The three lexemes are not philologically cognate but mark a structural-thematic cross-corpus cluster: each tradition independently develops a flood-vessel-vocabulary with distinct hull-form-specifications. See existing central entry `ma-gur-eleppu-tevah-flood-vessel-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: Abandon (your) possessions — seek (out) life!
Cast off acquisitions — keep (your) life alive!

lines.translit: šūli-ma zēr napšāti kalāma ana libbi eleppi

i18n.en: Bring aboard the seed of all living things into the boat.
The boat that you will build —
let her dimensions be measured (precisely);
let her breadth and her length be equal.

lines.commentary: The cube-form specification: equal breadth-and-length, paired with the *kīma apsî šullim-ši ṣūlul-ši* 'like the apsû, make her roof complete' of the next line (height-equals-side). The Mesopotamian-cubic vs Hebrew-rectangular hull-form is one of the structural divergences between the two flood-traditions — see new central entry `flood-vessel-construction-cubic-vs-rectangular-gilgamesh-genesis-cross-corpus`. The cubic eleppu (60 × 60 × 60 m ≈ 200,000 m³) contrasts with the rectangular tevah of Gen 6:14-16 (300 × 50 × 30 cubits ≈ 137 × 23 × 14 m ≈ 44,000 m³); the Hebrew theological-architectural framing of the tevah as a floating-temple-prototype (Wenham 1987 WBC) is absent from the Mesopotamian cube-form.

i18n.en: Like the apsû, make her (under-)roof complete."

lines.translit: anāku idēma azakkara ana Ea bēlī-ya

i18n.en: I understood, and I spoke to Ea my lord:
"The word of my lord — thus I have heeded it.
I have understood; I shall (do the work). But what shall I answer
(when) the city, the populace, and the elders (ask me)?"
Ea opened his mouth and spoke,
he said to me — to his servant:
"You — thus shall you say to them:
'Enlil has come to hate me —
I cannot dwell (any longer) in your city,

lines.translit: ina qaqqar Enlil ul ašakkana šēpī-ya

i18n.en: on Enlil's earth I cannot set my foot.

lines.translit: ur-rad-ma ana apsî it-ti Ea bēlī-ya ašab

i18n.en: I shall go down to the apsû — I shall dwell with Ea my lord.'
(But) upon you he will rain down abundance:

lines.commentary: The famous equivocal-omen: *nuḫšu* 'abundance' is paired in the next verse with *kukkū* — which can mean either 'cakes' (the surface, listener-on-the-spot reading) or 'darkness/disaster' (the cosmic-reader's-reading). The Mesopotamian Ea-doubletalk technique surfaces here in its most-cited example; cross-corpus to Greek-oracle ambiguity (e.g., Croesus' *if you cross the Halys you will destroy a great empire*) and to Hebrew prophetic-ambiguity (e.g., Jonah 3:4 *nehpāket*).

i18n.en: a bounty of birds, a hoard of fishes,
[he will set up] a harvest of richness.

lines.translit: ina šēr kukkī ina līlâti ušaznan-kunūši šamûtū kibāti

i18n.en: At dawn he will rain down cakes upon you; in the evening — a rain of wheat."
As soon as the first light of morning gleamed,

lines.translit: ina pī nāri pa-ḫi-ir mātu ana muḫḫi-ya

i18n.en: at the mouth of the river the land gathered to me.
[The craftsman] brought his axe;
the strong-armed brought their reed-mats and adzes;
the [young men] hauled the pitch; the able-bodied brought what was needed.
On the fifth day I laid down her hull.
Her floor was one ikû (= field-measure); her sides one kibru each.

lines.commentary: The Akkadian *ikû* (Sumerian-loan *iku*) is a field-measure — the area of a square approximately 60 × 60 m, ≈ 1 hectare. The floor-area of the boat is approximately 1 hectare; the *kibru* sides match the floor. George 2003 (vol. 1 512-518) calculates the cubic-vessel as approximately 60 m × 60 m × 60 m ≈ 200,000 m³. The unit-rendering convention (preserve *ikû* untranslated with a bracketed gloss) is documented at the overlay-entry `iku-nindan-mesopotamian-flood-boat-dimension-units-tablet-xi-53-55`. The Finkel 2014 *Atra-Hasis tablet* (BM 78941+) specifies a similar one-*ikû* base but with a round-coracle hull — a third Mesopotamian hull-tradition.

i18n.en: Ten nindan each was the height of her walls;
ten nindan each measured her sides.
I laid down her framework — I drew up her design.
I roofed her over with six (decks);

lines.commentary: The deck-structure: six decks here, divided into seven compartments at XI:58, with the interior subdivided into nine at XI:59. The Mesopotamian seven-deck vessel contrasts with the Hebrew three-deck *tevah* (Gen 6:16 — *tachtiyim shniyim u-shlishim* 'lower, second, and third'). Cross-corpus structural divergence; documented at the new central entry `flood-vessel-construction-cubic-vs-rectangular-gilgamesh-genesis-cross-corpus`. George 2003 vol. 1 510-518 treats the seven-vs-three deck-count crux.

i18n.en: I divided her into seven (compartments).
Her interior I divided into nine.

lines.translit: šigarī kīma ša mê amḫaṣ ina qabli-ša

i18n.en: Water-plugs I drove into her middle;
I provided the punt-poles and stored up the supplies.
Three šar of bitumen I poured into the kiln;

lines.commentary: Akkadian *kupru* (written ESIR.UD.A) is the bitumen / pitch waterproofing-substance — *directly Semitic-cognate* with Hebrew *kōfer* at Gen 6:14 (*va-kafarta otah mi-bayit u-mi-chutz ba-kofer*). The cognation derives from proto-Semitic *√kpr* and is one of the clearest lexical-cognate evidences for shared Mesopotamian-Hebrew flood-vocabulary. Documented at the new central entry `kupru-koper-bitumen-pitch-flood-boat-waterproofing-cross-corpus`. The Hebrew tradition extends the *kpr* root to develop the *atonement* / *kapporet* / *Yom Kippur* theological-lexicon — a Hebrew-internal semantic-development from the shared concrete-substance base.

i18n.en: three šar of asphalt I poured into her interior.
Three šar more (of bitumen) the basket-carriers brought up;

lines.translit: e-zib ŠÁR šamni ša anāku akula-ma

i18n.en: apart from a šar of oil that I myself consumed (in the work),
(and) two šar of oil the boatman stowed away.
For the workmen I slaughtered oxen;
I killed sheep day by day.

lines.translit: šikara kurunna šamna karāna ana ummâni

i18n.en: Beer, kurunnu-beer, oil, wine — to the workmen
I gave (these) to drink as if they were river-water.
I held a festival as if it were the akītu (= the New Year festival);

lines.commentary: *akītu* — the Babylonian New Year festival, the supreme cultic-celebration of the Mesopotamian liturgical year (Cohen 1993 *The Cultic Calendars of the Ancient Near East*). The simile frames Utnapishtim's pre-flood feast for the boat-builders as a *cosmic-festival-of-the-end-of-the-old-year* — fitting because the flood is about to mark a cosmic-year-end and the post-flood is a cosmic-new-beginning.

i18n.en: [I poured] oil with my (own) hands.
By the [seventh] day the boat was complete.
Her [launching] was difficult.
They brought the launching-poles above and below;
until two-thirds of her had entered the water.
Whatever [I had] I loaded aboard her:
whatever I had of silver I loaded aboard her;
whatever I had of gold I loaded aboard her;

lines.translit: mim-ma īšû zēr napšāti kalāma uštēli ana libbi-ša

i18n.en: whatever I had of the seed of all living things I brought aboard her.

lines.translit: uštēli ana libbi eleppi kala kimti-ya u salāti-ya

i18n.en: I brought aboard the boat all my family and my kin;

lines.translit: būl ṣēri umām ṣēri mārī ummâni kalī-šunu uštēli

i18n.en: the cattle of the field, the wild beasts of the field, and all the craftsmen — I brought aboard.

lines.commentary: The *mārī ummâni* — literally 'sons of the craftsman', the craftsman-class — loading is one of the most-distinctive elaborations of the Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh recension. The Sumerian Flood Story has Ziusudra board alone; the Atrahasis Epic has Atrahasis board with family and craftsmen (the precedent); Genesis 6-9 omits the craftsmen-loading entirely. The Hebrew tradition has eliminated the craftsmen-loading and entrusts post-flood civilization to a *rebuild-from-scratch* model — a theological choice that perhaps reflects the Hebrew suspicion of *technical-civilization* as a *Cainite* development (Gen 4:17-22). Documented at the new central entry `puzur-amurri-boat-pilot-craftsmen-loading-gilgamesh-xi-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: Shamash had set the appointed time:

lines.translit: ina šēr kukkī ina līlâti ušaznana šamûtū kibāti

i18n.en: "At dawn (he will rain down) cakes; in the evening he will rain upon you a rain of wheat.

lines.translit: erub ana libbi eleppi-ma pe-ḫi bāb-ki

i18n.en: Enter the boat — and seal up your door!"
That appointed time arrived.

lines.translit: ina šēr kukkī ina līlâti uš-az-na-an šamûtū kibāti

i18n.en: At dawn (it rained down) cakes; in the evening there fell a rain of wheat.
I watched the changing face of the day-weather;
the day, when omens were read, looked ominous indeed.

lines.translit: pa-la-ḫa-an-ni-ma ana libbi eleppi e-ru-ub-ma e-te-di-il bābī

i18n.en: I was afraid — I entered the boat and sealed up my doors.

lines.commentary: **Major theological divergence-site.** In Gilgamesh XI Utnapishtim seals the door himself; cross-corpus to Gen 7:16 *va-yisgōr YHWH baʿadô* — *and YHWH shut him in*. The Hebrew narrative has the deity actively close Noah's door; the Mesopotamian narrative has the human protagonist do it. The divergence encodes different theological-anthropologies: the Mesopotamian narrative emphasizes human-initiative-and-responsibility; the Hebrew narrative emphasizes divine-care-and-providence. Named-scholarship: Heidel 1946, Wenham 1987 WBC ad loc.

i18n.en: For the sealing-up of the boat,
to Puzur-Amurri the boatman

lines.commentary: Puzur-Amurri is a theophoric proper-name: *puzur* 'secret, hidden thing' + *Amurri* (genitive of *Amurru*, the West-Semitic deity Amurru, patron of the Amorite people) — *Secret-of-Amurru*. The named boatman is distinctive to the Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh recension; absent from the Sumerian Flood Story, the Atrahasis Epic, and Genesis 6-9. Sin-leqi-unninni's literary-distinctive. Documented at the new central entry `puzur-amurri-boat-pilot-craftsmen-loading-gilgamesh-xi-cross-corpus` and the overlay-entry `puzur-amurri-named-boatman-rendering-convention`.

i18n.en: I handed over the palace together with its goods.
As soon as the first light of morning gleamed,

lines.translit: i-lam-ma iš-tu i-šid šamê ur-pa-tu ṣa-lim-tum

i18n.en: from the horizon of heaven there rose up a black cloud.
Within it Adad was thundering;

lines.commentary: Adad — the Mesopotamian-Akkadian storm-god — is the flood-instrument: his thunder unleashes the seven-day storm. Adad is **etymologically-cognate** with the Northwest-Semitic *Hadad / Hadda* (Ugaritic *Haddu*, the standing-epithet of Baʿlu in the Baal Cycle); the two are the same storm-deity across adjacent linguistic-traditions. The Mesopotamian Adad-as-flood-instrument is the precedent for the wider Northwest-Semitic *storm-god-as-cosmic-cataclysm* trope that recurs in the Hebrew YHWH-as-storm-god typology (Ps 29, Ps 18:7-15, Hab 3). Documented at the new central entry `adad-hadad-baal-storm-god-flood-instrument-cross-corpus`.

lines.translit: Šullat u Ḫaniš illakū ina maḫri

i18n.en: Shullat and Hanish went forth as heralds —
the throne-bearers went out over mountain and land.
Errakal tore out the mooring-poles;
Ninurta went forth — he caused the (dyke-)dams to overflow.
The Anunnaki raised up their torches;

lines.commentary: **Acknowledgment-without-endorsement site.** The Anunnaki (Akkadian collective-noun for the high-and/or-chthonic gods; from Sumerian *a-nun-na* 'those of princely seed') are among the two principal magnet-terms (alongside *apkallu*) for popular-fringe ancient-astronaut and extraterrestrial-civilization interpretive overlays — most prominently the Zecharia Sitchin *The 12th Planet* (1976) tradition and its successors. The Akkadian source-text deploys the standard theological-mythological vocabulary of divine-classes (Anunnaki: high gods / chthonic gods; Igigi: heavenly gods) per Black-Green 1992 *Gods, Demons and Symbols*; no engineering-protocol vocabulary is present. The WoH acknowledgment-without-endorsement framework (parallel to the Shi'ur Qomah parasangs precedent) is documented at the new central entry `anunnaki-igigi-mesopotamian-divine-classes-popular-fringe-acknowledgment-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: with their bright radiance they set the land ablaze.
Adad's paralyzing-terror passed over the heavens;
whatever was bright he turned to darkness.
The land was shattered like a pot.
For one day the storm-wind blew.
Swiftly it blew — [against the mountains it bore down]: the flood!

lines.translit: ki-ma qabli eli nišī i-ba-aʾ kašūšu

i18n.en: Like a battle it came over the people — the cataclysm.

lines.commentary: *kašūšu* — the divine annihilation-instrument / disaster-weapon. The lexeme is a strong cosmic-cataclysm marker; the *kīma qabli* 'like a battle' simile compares the flood to military-combat. The flood-as-cosmic-warfare framing recurs in Mesopotamian flood-tradition (Atrahasis III; cf. *abubu mēhû qabla* 'flood-storm-(war-like)-cataclysm' at XI:127).

i18n.en: Brother could not see his brother;
people could not be recognized from the sky (above).
The gods (themselves) were afraid of the flood;

lines.translit: it-ḫi-šum-ma i-te-lu-ú ana šamê ša Anim

i18n.en: they shrank back, they fled up to the heaven of Anu.

lines.commentary: The gods retreat to *šamê ša Anim* — *the heaven of Anu* — the highest cosmographic-zone of the Mesopotamian three-tier cosmos (heaven of Anu / heaven of Enlil / heaven of Ea-Apsû). The image of the gods *fleeing* their own flood-decision sets up the divine-vulnerability climax at XI:113.

lines.translit: ilānu ki-ma kalbi kun-nu-nu ina kamāti rab-ṣu

i18n.en: The gods cowered like dogs, crouching against the outer wall.

lines.commentary: One of the literary climaxes of Tablet XI. *ilānu kīma kalbi kunnunu ina kamāti rabṣu* — the gods themselves are *afraid of the flood* (XI:111), have *fled up to the heaven of Anu* (XI:112), and are now reduced to *fearful animals crouching against the cosmic outer-wall*. The Mesopotamian theology of *divine-vulnerability* is here at its most striking. Genesis 6-9 has no equivalent divine-fear or divine-cowering moment; the Hebrew tradition has eliminated the divine-vulnerability motif, paralleling its elimination of the divine-hunger motif at Gen 8:21. Documented at the new central entry `gods-cower-like-dogs-cosmic-wall-gilgamesh-xi-113-literary-marker-cross-corpus`. Named-scholarship: Foster 2005, George 2003, Heidel 1946 chap. 4, Westermann 1984.

i18n.en: Ishtar cried out like a woman in childbirth;

lines.commentary: The cosmic-anguish simile. Standard ANE birth-pang vocabulary for cosmic-distress (cf. Isa 13:8, 21:3, Jer 4:31, Mic 4:9-10 — the Hebrew prophetic-corpus extends the same birth-pang trope to political-cosmic crisis). Ishtar's lament continues through XI:115-121, where she regrets having spoken evil in the divine-assembly — the gods' decision to send the flood now strikes her as the unmaking of her own people whom she 'birthed' (XI:120-121).

lines.translit: ú-na-am-ba bēltu ša ilī ṭābat rigma

i18n.en: the Lady of the Gods, sweet of voice, wailed aloud:

lines.translit: ūmu ulli-tu ana ṭiṭṭi lū i-tu-ur-ma

i18n.en: "Would that the (former) day had (instead) turned to clay,

lines.translit: aššu anāku ina puḫur ilāni aqbû lemnêti

i18n.en: since I myself spoke evil in the assembly of the gods!

lines.translit: ki-i aqbû ina puḫur ilāni lemnêti

i18n.en: How could I have spoken evil in the assembly of the gods —
calling for a battle (= the flood) to destroy my (own) people!
I myself bore (= gave birth to) my (own) people;
like the spawn of fishes they fill the sea!"
The Anunnaki-gods wept along with her;
the gods sat (down) in mourning.
Their lips were covered over, parched (with grief).
For six days and seven nights

lines.commentary: The famous Babylonian flood-duration formula: *six days and seven nights*. Cross-corpus to the Sumerian Flood Story (*seven days and seven nights*; FLS-WOH-D:3) and Atrahasis III.iv.24-25 (*seven days seven nights*). The slightly-variant Gilgamesh six-and-seven (vs. Atrahasis seven-and-seven) is a recognized text-critical observation (George 2003 vol. 1 510-519). The major cross-corpus divergence is with Hebrew Gen 7:12 — *forty days and forty nights* — the Hebrew *typological-intensification* by approximately the Mesopotamian-7 × 6 = Hebrew-40. Treated at the existing central entry `seven-day-flood-vs-forty-day-flood-duration-tradition-cross-corpus`, extended in this editor pass.

lines.translit: il-lak šāru abūbu mēḫû i-sa-pan māta

i18n.en: the wind blew — the flood, the storm — and levelled the land.

lines.translit: ina 7-šu kašād(i) ūmi i-nu-uḫ abūbu mēḫû qabla

i18n.en: When the seventh day arrived, the flood, the storm, the (war-like) cataclysm abated.
(The storm) which had battled like a woman in labour —
the sea grew quiet; it became still.
The evil-wind, the flood, ceased.

lines.commentary: *imḫullu* — the destructive cosmic-wind. The same lexeme appears in Enuma Elish IV.96 as one of Marduk's seven weapons in the Tiamat-combat (*in his mouth he set the imḫullu / the evil-wind*); in Atrahasis III.iii.18-19 as the flood-storm; here as the flood-cessation. Existing central entry `im-hul-imhullu-destructive-storm-wind-mesopotamian-storm-vocabulary-cross-corpus` extended in this editor pass to include this refId.

i18n.en: I looked out at the day: its sound was stilled,

lines.translit: u kullat tenēšeti i-tu-ra ana ṭiṭṭi

i18n.en: and all of humanity had turned (back) to clay.

lines.commentary: Humans return to *ṭiṭṭu* — clay — the substance from which they were originally formed in the Mesopotamian creation-traditions (Atrahasis I, *Enki and Ninmah*). Cross-corpus to Hebrew Gen 3:19 *ki afar atah v-el afar tashuv* — *for dust you are, and to dust you shall return*; existing central entry `return-to-the-earth-mortality-verdict-adapa-genesis-cross-corpus` covers the broader cross-corpus.

i18n.en: (The flood-plain) was flat as a roof.

lines.translit: ap-te nappišta-ma ṣētu ūmma im-ta-qut eli dūr appī-ya

i18n.en: I opened a vent — and daylight fell upon the side of my nose.

lines.translit: uš-qam-ma-ma ki-mi-iṣ-ya eli appī-ya il-li-ku dīm-tum

i18n.en: I bowed down, I knelt, I wept; down the side of my nose the tears flowed.
I looked out across the world-quarters: (the world had become) the edge of the sea.
At (a distance of) twelve (leagues), a region rose up.
On Mount Nimush the boat came to rest;

lines.commentary: **Mountain-landing site, major cross-corpus.** The Akkadian *KUR Nimuš* (George 2003's reading; older Thompson 1930 / Heidel 1946 read *KUR Niṣir*). The reading-crux is documented at the overlay-entry `mount-nimush-vs-mount-nisir-manuscript-variant-rendering-convention`. The geographic identification (Pir Omar Gudrun range in the modern Iraqi-Kurdistan Zagros foothills) is preserved across both readings. Three-way cross-corpus: Mt Nimush (Gilgamesh XI:138); the *mountains of Ararat* (Gen 8:4 — note the Hebrew *plural* *harei*, a mountainous-region not a single peak); al-Jūdī (Qur'an 11:44; classically identified with Cudi Dağı in southeastern Anatolia). Three traditions, one fixed narrative-slot, three distinct named mountains. Documented at the new central entry `mt-nimush-nisir-ararat-judi-flood-mountain-landing-cross-corpus`. Also relates to the broader Northwest-Semitic cosmic-mountain tradition (Mount Ṣapunu of Baʿlu, Mount Sinai / Horeb of YHWH) — see existing central entries `mount-sapunu-tsafon-cosmic-mountain-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bible` and `har-sinai-horev-the-mountain-of-Elohim-divine-mountain-cross-corpus`, both extended in this editor pass.

lines.translit: šadû Nimuš eleppa iṣbat-ma a-na nâši ul iddin

i18n.en: Mount Nimush held the boat fast — it did not let it move.
One day, two days, Mount Nimuš [held the boat fast];
three days, four days, Mount Nimuš [held the boat fast];

lines.translit: 5 ūma 6 ūmī šadû Nimuš iṣbat-ma ana nâši ul iddin

i18n.en: five days, six days, Mount Nimuš held the boat fast — it did not let it move.
When the seventh day arrived,
I brought out a dove and released (it).

lines.commentary: **The bird-test sequence opens — major cross-corpus.** Gilgamesh-XI order: **dove → swallow → raven** (XI:144-152), with the raven *last* and its non-return signalling the flood's end. Cross-corpus Gen 8:6-12 inverts the order: **raven → dove → dove → dove**, with the raven *first* and the third dove's non-return signalling the flood's end. The Hebrew tradition has also added the *olive-leaf-in-the-dove's-mouth* (Gen 8:11), a Hebrew-distinctive literary feature with no Mesopotamian precedent. The Qur'anic tradition (Q 11:42-43) substitutes a different test entirely: Noah's son refuses embarkation. Three traditions, one fixed bird-test narrative-slot, three distinct deployments. Documented at the new central entry `bird-test-flood-narrative-cross-corpus-gilgamesh-genesis-qur-an`.

i18n.en: The dove went forth, (and) came back;
no resting-place appeared — and she returned.
I brought out a swallow and released (it).
The swallow went forth, (and) came back;
no resting-place appeared — and she returned.
I brought out a raven and released (it).
The raven went forth, saw the receding of the waters;
it ate, it foraged, it cawed (?) — it did not return.

lines.commentary: The raven's *non-return* signals the flood's end in the Mesopotamian tradition. Cross-corpus Gen 8:12 — the third *dove's* non-return signals the flood's end in the Hebrew tradition. Same narrative-function, different bird-species, different order in the test-sequence.

i18n.en: I brought (all) out — and to the four winds I made an offering.

lines.commentary: The four cardinal-winds (treated at existing central entry `shutu-cardinal-winds-akkadian-four-winds-divinized-cross-corpus`) are the divinized atmospheric-zones; the offering-to-the-four-winds is the cosmographic-orientation-and-thanksgiving move. Cross-corpus to Hebrew *arba kanfot ha-aretz* 'four corners of the earth' (Isa 11:12, Ezek 7:2) — the same four-direction cosmographic structure.

lines.translit: aš-kun sur-qe-nu eli zikkurati ša šadî

i18n.en: I set up an incense-offering upon the ziggurat of the mountain (-peak).

lines.commentary: The cult-architecture term *ziqqurratu* — temple-tower-stepped-pyramid — is here applied to a *natural mountain-peak* as natural-temple. The post-flood sacrifice transforms the landing-mountain into a cosmic-sanctuary. Cross-corpus to Gen 8:20 (Noah builds an *altar* — *mizbeach* — without the natural-temple-of-mountain elaboration). The Mesopotamian ziggurat-on-mountain pairs the cult-architecture with the cosmic-mountain (see existing central entry `mount-sapunu-tsafon-cosmic-mountain-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bible`, extended in this pass).

i18n.en: Seven and seven cult-vessels (adagurrū) I set up;

lines.commentary: The fourteen-vessel formula (*7 + 7*). Cross-corpus to Gen 7:2 — *miqkol ha-behemah ha-tehorah tiqqach lekha shivah shivah ish v-ishto* — *of every clean beast you shall take seven pairs (literally 'seven seven') male and female*. The sacred-seven-and-seven recurs across the Mesopotamian and Hebrew flood-traditions; the Akkadian *adagurru* is a clay cult-vessel for libations (specifically the post-flood thanksgiving-offering).

lines.translit: ina šap-li-šu-nu at-bu-uk qanâ ereni u asu

i18n.en: beneath them I poured out reed, cedar, and myrtle.
The gods smelled the savor;
the gods smelled the sweet savor.

lines.commentary: **Direct lexical-and-semantic cross-corpus parallel.** Akkadian *erīšu ṭābu* ('sweet savor') = Hebrew *reach ha-nichoach* ('pleasing aroma', Gen 8:21) — among the strongest Mesopotamian-Hebrew lexical-cognate cross-corpus parallels. The construction *the gods smelled the sweet savor* parallels Hebrew *va-yarach YHWH et reach ha-nichoach* nearly word-for-word. The next line (XI:159) is where the two traditions diverge: the Mesopotamian gods crowd the smoke *like flies*; the Hebrew YHWH is decoupled from the divine-hunger. Existing central entry `post-flood-thanksgiving-sacrifice-trope-cross-corpus` extended in this pass; new central entry `gods-like-flies-vs-pleasing-aroma-flood-sacrifice-cross-corpus` documents the divergence.

lines.translit: ilānu kīma zumbī eli bēl niqê ip-taḫ-ru

i18n.en: The gods gathered like flies around the (lord-of-the-)sacrifice.

lines.commentary: **Critical cross-corpus divergence — the gods-like-flies vs YHWH's-pleasing-aroma contrast.** *ilānu kīma zumbī eli bēl niqê iptaḫru* — the famous post-flood divine-hunger image. The Mesopotamian gods have *starved* during the seven-day flood (no humans = no sacrifices = no fed gods) and now crowd Utnapishtim's offering *like flies*. Atrahasis III v 30-35 deploys the same image. Cross-corpus Gen 8:21 — *va-yarach YHWH et reach ha-nichoach* — YHWH *smells the pleasing aroma* and is pleased; the Hebrew tradition has eliminated the divine-hunger and the fly-image, decoupling YHWH from the *need* for offerings while preserving the aesthetic-relational smell-of-the-offering trope. The lexical-near-cognation of Akkadian *erīšu ṭābu* (XI:158) with Hebrew *reach ha-nichoach* proves Hebrew dependence; the elimination of the fly-image proves Hebrew theological-reshaping. Documented at the new central entry `gods-like-flies-vs-pleasing-aroma-flood-sacrifice-cross-corpus`. The *bēl niqê* 'lord-of-the-(sacrificer-)offering' construct-rendering convention is documented at the overlay-entry `tablet-xi-bel-niqe-lord-of-the-sacrifice-rendering-convention`.

lines.translit: iš-tu ul-la-nu-um-ma bēltu rabītu ina kašādi-ša

i18n.en: From of old, (when) the Great Lady was arriving,

lines.translit: ul-li nimēqī rabûti ša Anum īpu-šu kī ṣubāti-ya

i18n.en: she lifted up the great lapis-lazuli (necklace) which Anu had made for her as a (love-)token:

lines.commentary: Ishtar's lapis-lazuli necklace functions in Tablet XI as Yahweh's rainbow functions in Gen 9:13. The colored-arc-shaped divine-object set in the cosmos as a *post-flood memorial / covenantal-sign*: in the Mesopotamian narrative, the lapis-necklace lifted up by Ishtar; in the Hebrew narrative, the *qeshet* 'bow / rainbow' (Gen 9:12-17). Both function as eternal mnemonic of the flood-survivor's preservation; both involve a *divine commitment never to forget* (XI:162-163 — *lū la amaš-ši* 'let me not forget'; Gen 9:15 — *v-zakharti et briti*). Named-scholarship: Heidel 1946, George 2003, Wenham 1987 WBC.

lines.translit: ilānu annūti lū lapis-uknī ina kišādī-ya lū la amaš-ši

i18n.en: "O these (jewels) — let (these) lapis-lazuli at my neck (be the sign): I shall not forget!

lines.translit: ūmī annûti lū aḫsus-su ana dāri lū la amaš-ši

i18n.en: These days let me remember — for ever, let me not forget!
Let the gods come to the incense-offering!
But let Enlil not come to the incense-offering —

lines.commentary: Ishtar's exclusion of Enlil from the post-flood thanksgiving — *aššu la im-tal-ku-ma iškuna a-bu-ba* 'because, without taking counsel, he brought on the flood' (XI:166) — opens the divine-confrontation that will lead to Utnapishtim's deification (XI:191-198). Enlil arrives, sees the boat, flies into a rage (XI:169-170), is rebuked by Ninurta and Ea (XI:173-190), and finally reverses his rage with the deification-blessing.

i18n.en: because, without taking counsel, he brought on the flood,
and consigned my (own) people to destruction."
As soon as Enlil arrived,
he saw the boat — and Enlil flew into a rage.
He was filled with fury against the Igigi-gods:

lines.commentary: **Acknowledgment-without-endorsement site.** The Igigi (Akkadian collective-noun for the heavenly gods; lower-tier in the divine-class hierarchy in contrast to the high-and-chthonic Anunnaki) is the second principal magnet-term in the divine-class register. Black-Green 1992 *Gods, Demons and Symbols* treats the scholarly classical reading; the WoH acknowledgment-without-endorsement framework on the popular-fringe ET-civilization reception is documented at the new central entry `anunnaki-igigi-mesopotamian-divine-classes-popular-fringe-acknowledgment-cross-corpus`.

i18n.en: "Has anyone (here) come out alive?
No man was to have survived the destruction!"
Ninurta the warrior answered and spoke
to the warrior Enlil:

lines.translit: man-nu-um-ma ša lā Ea i-ban-na-a a-ma-ta

i18n.en: "Who but Ea could (have) devise(d) this matter?
And Ea — he knows every (kind of) craft."
Ea the warrior answered and spoke
to the warrior Enlil:
"You, sage of the gods, warrior —

lines.commentary: Ea is addressed as *apkal ilāni* — *sage of the gods*. The *apkallu* lexeme that elsewhere names the seven antediluvian sages (Adapa-Uan etc.) is here applied to Ea himself as the divine-patron of the sage-tradition. Cross-reference to the closing-line at XI:308 (the *Seven Sages* who lay Uruk's foundations) — the apkallu-tradition frames both the opening and closing of the flood-narrative. Existing central entry `adapa-apkallu-first-antediluvian-sage-paradigm-cross-corpus` extended in this editor pass.

lines.translit: ki-i ki-i lā tam-tal-lik-ma a-bu-ba taš-kun

i18n.en: how, oh how, without taking counsel, did you bring on a flood?!
Lay the sin upon the sinner;

lines.commentary: **The proportionality-principle.** *bēl ḫīṭīti emid ḫīṭa-šu* (XI:181) / *bēl gillati emid gillata-šu* (XI:182) — *lay the sin on the sinner; lay the trespass on the trespasser*. One of the earliest extant divine-justice-as-proportionate articulations in ANE literature; Ea is here arguing against collective-punishment (the flood that killed everyone) in favor of individualized-responsibility-and-judgment. Cross-corpus to Ezek 18:20 *ha-nefesh ha-chotet hi tamut* — *the soul that sins, it shall die* — the foundational Hebrew articulation of individual-responsibility against the inherited-guilt model of Exod 20:5; also Deut 24:16 (children not punished for fathers' sins; nor fathers for children's). Named-scholarship: Greenberg 1980 on Ezek 18; George 2003 and Foster 2005 on the Tablet-XI line as the *pre-history* of the Hebrew tradition.

i18n.en: lay the trespass upon the trespasser.
Relent — that he be not cut off; pull back — that he be not unsettled!

lines.translit: ki-i lā taš-ku-na a-bu-ba nēšu lit-bā-ma nišī liṣaḫḫir

i18n.en: Instead of bringing on a flood, let a lion arise and diminish the people!

lines.commentary: Ea's catalogue of proportionate-alternative-judgments (XI:184-187): lion / wolf / famine / Erra (pestilence). Each is a *measured* divine-response that would diminish but not eliminate humanity. The catalogue extends the proportionality-principle of XI:181-182 into specific population-control options; the parallel with the Atrahasis tradition (where the gods deploy plague, drought, famine *before* the flood) is striking — Ea is here naming the *Atrahasis-tradition alternatives* as the options Enlil should have used.

lines.translit: ki-i lā taš-ku-na a-bu-ba barbara lit-bā-ma nišī liṣaḫḫir

i18n.en: Instead of bringing on a flood, let a wolf arise and diminish the people!

lines.translit: ki-i lā taš-ku-na a-bu-ba ḫušaḫḫu liššakin-ma māta li-iš-[gi-iš]

i18n.en: Instead of bringing on a flood, let famine be set up and [lay waste] the land!

lines.translit: ki-i lā taš-ku-na a-bu-ba dErra lit-bā-ma māta liš-giš

i18n.en: Instead of bringing on a flood, let Erra arise and lay waste the land!

lines.translit: anāku ul ap-ta-a piriš-ti ilī rabûti

i18n.en: I did not (myself) reveal the secret of the great gods —

lines.commentary: Ea's defense: technically he did not reveal the secret directly — he caused a *dream* to appear to Atra-ḫasīs (XI:189), and the secret was *heard* through the dream-medium. The loophole-argument allows Ea to escape oath-violation charges. The Ea-warning-via-dream variant (Atrahasis-tradition device) is here invoked to dodge the Ea-warning-via-reed-wall reading of XI:20-22. The deception-misadvice-test crux of the Ea-warning is documented at the existing central entry `ea-warning-deception-misadvice-test-crux-cross-corpus`.

lines.translit: atra-ḫasīs šunatti ušabri-šum-ma piriš-ti ilī iš-me

i18n.en: to Atra-ḫasīs I caused a dream to appear, and (so) the secret of the gods he heard.

lines.commentary: Utnapishtim is here named *Atra-ḫasīs* — 'Surpassingly Wise' — the same name as the protagonist of the Akkadian Atrahasis Epic (Lambert and Millard 1969). The Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh tradition is here signalling that its flood-survivor is the same character as the Atrahasis flood-survivor, only under his alternative standing-epithet *Utnapishtim* ('I-found-life') vs. *Atra-ḫasīs* ('Surpassingly-Wise'). The Ea-warning-via-dream variant (Atrahasis tradition) is distinct from the Ea-warning-via-the-reed-wall (Gilgamesh-XI:20-22); Ea's defense to Enlil at XI:188-189 effectively claims he never directly revealed the secret — the *dream* of Atra-ḫasīs is the loophole-evidence. The Atra-ḫasīs alias-preservation convention is documented at the overlay-entry `atra-hasis-alias-preservation-tablet-xi-189`.

i18n.en: Now, then — take counsel for him (= Utnapishtim)!"
Enlil went up into the boat;
he took me by the hand and brought me up onto the deck.
He brought up — he made my wife sit beside me;

lines.translit: u-lap-pit putta-ni i-zi-iz ina bi-ri-ni i-ka-ar-ra-ban-na-ši

i18n.en: he touched our foreheads, stood between us, and blessed us:
"In times past, Utnapishtim was (only) human;

lines.commentary: Enlil's blessing opens with the *human / no-longer-human* before/after structure that frames the deification. The *amēlu-tam-ma* 'human-only / just human' construction sets up the *kī ilāni nâši* 'like us, the gods' of the following line. The Akkadian *amēlu* is the standard humankind-lexeme; the *only* / *just* sense surfaces from the temporal-contrast.

lines.translit: i-na-an-na Ūta-napišti u sinništu-šu lū e-mu-u kī ilāni nâši

i18n.en: now let Utnapishtim and his wife become like us, the gods!

lines.commentary: **The deification line.** *lū emû kī ilāni nâši* — *let them become like us, the gods*. Cross-corpus Gen 3:22 — *hen ha-adam hayah k-achad mimennu la-da'at tov va-ra* — *behold, the human has become like one of us, knowing good and bad*. The same theological-recognition (humans entering the divine-knowledge-and-status category) receives **opposite divine-responses**: in Gilgamesh-XI, deification-by-reward; in Genesis, expulsion-from-Eden and barring-of-the-tree-of-life. The cross-corpus *structural-inversion* — Mesopotamian won-immortality (Gilgamesh-XI) vs Mesopotamian lost-immortality (Adapa) vs Hebrew acquired-wisdom-then-barred-immortality (Eden) — is documented at the new central entry `utnapishtim-deification-vs-adapa-immortality-loss-cross-corpus`. All three narratives reach the same end-state for humanity-in-general (wisdom-bearing-but-mortal); Utnapishtim is the *exception* that proves the rule.

lines.translit: lū-ši-ib Ūta-napišti ina rūqi ina pī nārāti

i18n.en: Let Utnapishtim dwell far away, at the mouth of the rivers!"

lines.commentary: *pī nārāti* 'mouth of the rivers' is the cosmic-periphery, the *edge of the world* where the deified Utnapishtim is settled. Cross-corpus parallels: the Hebrew Eden as river-source (Gen 2:10-14, the four rivers); Greek Hesperides at the far west; the *Islands of the Blest* tradition in Hesiod and later Greek thought; the Sumerian Dilmun as *clean / paradisal land* (existing central entry `dilmun-eastern-paradise-cross-corpus`). The *immortal-flood-survivor-settled-at-the-edge-of-the-world* tradition is one of the most-developed comparative-mythology motifs (West 1997 *East Face of Helicon*).

lines.translit: il-qu-šu-in-ni-ma ina rūqi ina pī nārāti uš-bu-ʾi-in-ni

i18n.en: They took me — at the mouth of the rivers, far away, they settled me.

lines.translit: i-nu-ma ka-a-ša mannu ana ka-a-ša ilāni upaḫḫar-ma

i18n.en: Now — as for you, (Gilgamesh) — who will gather the gods together for your sake,
that you may find the (eternal) life you seek?

lines.translit: alka — 6 ūmī u 7 mušâti la taṣallal

i18n.en: Come now — for six days and seven nights do not sleep!"

lines.commentary: The sleep-test deploys the same six-and-seven temporal-formula as the flood-duration (XI:125, 127, 142). Sacred-seven is corpus-wide across the Mesopotamian narrative-time vocabulary: seven-day flood-storm; seven-day rest-on-mountain (XI:143); seven days the dove-test (XI:144, in some readings); seven-loaves-catalogue here. Cross-corpus to the seven-day Hebrew creation-week (Gen 1), seven-day mourning (Gen 50:10, 1 Sam 31:13), Atrahasis 7-day construction.

i18n.en: But as he sat upon the threshold,
sleep, like mist, enveloped him.

lines.translit: Ūta-napišti izakkara ana šâši ana sinništi-šu

i18n.en: Utnapishtim spoke to her — to his wife:
"Behold the young man who sought (eternal) life!
Sleep, like mist, has enveloped him."

lines.translit: sinništu izakkara ana šâšu ana Ūta-napišti rūqi

i18n.en: (His) wife spoke to him — to Utnapishtim the Distant:
"Touch him — let the man wake!

lines.translit: ḫarrāna ša illika lū ina šal-mim li-tu-ra

i18n.en: Let the road by which he came return him (home) in peace;

lines.translit: [ina] bāb ša u-ṣu-u li-tu-ra ana māti-šu

i18n.en: by the gate from which he went out, let him return to his land."

lines.translit: Ūta-napišti izakkara ana šâši ana sinništi-šu

i18n.en: Utnapishtim spoke to her — to his wife:
"Humanity is always deceiving — it will (yet) deceive you, too.

lines.translit: alki epi-šu-ma akala u šukni eli muḫḫi-šu

i18n.en: Come — bake him bread and set (it) by his head.

lines.translit: u ūmī ša iṣ-ṣa-lu-lu ina igāri ušan-ni

i18n.en: And the days that he sleeps — mark (them) on the wall."
She baked his loaves and set (them) by his head;

lines.translit: u ūmī ša iṣ-ṣa-lu-lu ina igāri uš-ta-an-ni-šu

i18n.en: and the days that he slept she marked upon the wall.
His first loaf was (already) dried out;

lines.commentary: The seven-loaves catalogue opens (XI:217-222). Each day's loaf measures the passage of time as Gilgamesh sleeps through Utnapishtim's deification-test (the *six days and seven nights without sleep* of XI:201). The literal day-by-day catalogue is preserved through XI:217-222 and recapitulated at XI:230-235; the structural parallelism encodes the narrative-significance.

i18n.en: the second was leathery; the third was soggy;
the fourth — its crust had turned white;
the fifth had cast a mould;
the sixth was (still freshly) baked;
the seventh — (still) on its coals — and (just then) he touched him.
The man woke up.

lines.translit: Gilgāmeš ana šâšu izakkara ana Ūta-napišti rūqi

i18n.en: Gilgamesh spoke to him — to Utnapishtim the Distant:
"Just as I was about to fall asleep — you touched me;
swiftly you touched me — and you woke me!"
Utnapishtim [spoke to him] — to Gilgamesh:
"Come, Gilgamesh — count your loaves!

lines.translit: u ūmī ša ta-aṣ-lu-lu lu-u i-du-šu-uš-ka

i18n.en: And the days that you slept — let them be known to you.
Your first loaf was (already) dried out;
the second leathery, the third soggy;
the fourth — its crust turned white;
the fifth had cast a mould;
the sixth was (still freshly) baked;

lines.translit: se-bu-u ina pi-in-ti-šu i-na pa-na-tu-uš-šu-ma lap-tat-ka

i18n.en: the seventh was on its coals — and just then I touched you."

lines.translit: Gilgāmeš ana šâšu izakkara ana Ūta-napišti rūqi

i18n.en: Gilgamesh spoke to him — to Utnapishtim the Distant:
"What shall I do, Utnapishtim — where shall I go?
A snatcher has seized my flesh;
in my bed-chamber Death dwells,

lines.commentary: Gilgamesh's mortality-confrontation: *mūtu* (Death) personified as inhabiting the most-private spaces (the bed-chamber, the path-of-the-foot). The Mesopotamian *mūtu*-personification cross-corpus to Ugaritic Mot (the Death-god of the Baal Cycle) and Hebrew Mawet personifications (Hos 13:14; Job 18:13-14). The lament announces the emotional-core of Gilgamesh's quest: not the literal-immortality but the unbearable-knowledge-of-death.

i18n.en: and wherever I set [my foot], there too is Death."

lines.translit: Ūta-napišti izakkara ana šâšu ana Ur-Šanabi malāḫi

i18n.en: Utnapishtim spoke to him — to Ur-Shanabi the boatman:
"Ur-Shanabi — may the harbor reject you, the crossing-place shun you!

lines.translit: ša ina aḫi-šu it-tal-la-ku zummâta aḫa-šu

i18n.en: You who walked along its (= the death-shore's) bank — forsake that bank (now).

lines.translit: amēlu ša tu-ub-la-an-na šuʾattim ina pā-ni-ka

i18n.en: The man whom you brought (here) — his body is shameful before you (unwashed).
Let his skin be cleansed — let the bloom of his (handsome) figure return to him;
let his garment be cast off — let it be clean.
Let the sea-waters bear (the old garment) away from him.
Let [his body] be made sound; let his head be made pure.

lines.translit: kar-bal-la-tu lu na-aš-šat ki-li-il-ši lu-tar-ri ana ṣē-ri-šu

i18n.en: Let a new turban be put upon (him); let the wraparound (robe) be restored to his back.
Until he goes to his (own) city,
until he travels his road,

lines.translit: kar-bal-la-tu ay i-tar-ru-uš kib-ba-šu lū eššâ-ma

i18n.en: let the turban not be taken off — let it be kept ever-new."
Ur-Shanabi took him and seated him at the wash-basin.

lines.translit: ma-aš-ka i-ki-šum-ma ina mê tâmtim it-bal

i18n.en: He washed his skin — and the waters of the sea bore (the filth) away.
So was his body made pure — and his head cleansed.
The garment of (old) skin was cast off — and the sea bore it away.
He put on the new turban; his wraparound was (made) new.

lines.translit: Gilgāmeš u Ur-Šanabi i-tab-ka-nim-ma ina eleppi ir-ka-bū

i18n.en: Gilgamesh and Ur-Shanabi (then) embarked; they sailed away in the boat.
They set the boat (loose) — they crossed over (the waters).

lines.translit: sinništu-šu ana šâšu ana Ūta-napišti rūqi

i18n.en: (His) wife (spoke) to him — to Utnapishtim the Distant:
"Gilgamesh came; he toiled; he laboured.
What will you give him, that he may return to his land?"
And he, Gilgamesh, raised up the punt-pole.
He drove the boat (back) toward the shore.

lines.translit: Ūta-napišti ana šâšu izakkara ana Gilgāmeš

i18n.en: Utnapishtim spoke to him — to Gilgamesh:
"Gilgamesh, you came; you toiled; you laboured.
What can I give you that you may return to your land?
Let me reveal to you, Gilgamesh, a hidden matter —

lines.translit: u piriš-ti ša ilāni kâ-ša luqbî-ka

i18n.en: and the secret of the gods let me tell you.
There is a plant — its appearance is like the boxthorn;

lines.commentary: **The plant of rejuvenation — major cross-corpus.** *šammu* — Akkadian noun for *plant / herb / drug-substance* (CAD Š/1 311-316). The plant whose acquisition would have given Gilgamesh *renewed life* (XI:273). Cross-corpus to the Hebrew tree-of-life (Gen 2:9, 3:22 — *etz ha-chayyim*) and to Qur'an 20:120 (the *shajara al-khuld* 'tree of immortality' shown to Adam by the devil). The Mesopotamian-Hebrew structural-inversion (Gilgamesh obtains-then-loses; Adam barred-from) is documented at the new central entry `plant-of-rejuvenation-shammu-serpent-loss-cross-corpus-gilgamesh-genesis`.

i18n.en: its thorns are like the brier-bush — they will prick your hand.
If your hands can obtain that plant,
[you will find] your (renewed) life."
When Gilgamesh heard this,

lines.translit: ip-tu-ú raṭ-ṭam(?) ina šēpē-šu it-mu-uḫ abnē kabtūti

i18n.en: he opened a channel(?); at his feet he tied heavy stones.
They drew him down (with their weight) into the apsû.

lines.commentary: Gilgamesh dives into the *apsû* — the cosmic freshwater abyss; Ea's cosmographic-domain. The existing central entry `abzu-engur-sumerian-subterranean-deep-cross-corpus` covers the Sumerian-Akkadian-Hebrew cross-corpus (Sumerian *abzu* → Akkadian *apsû* → Hebrew *tehom* 'the deep' of Gen 1:2). Gilgamesh's diving-with-weights is the technique of pearl-divers and abalone-divers in the Persian Gulf — a quasi-realistic detail in the otherwise mythological narrative.

i18n.en: He himself grasped the plant — and it pricked his hand.
He cut loose the heavy stones beneath him,
and the sea bore him up onto its shore.

lines.translit: Gilgāmeš ana šâšu izakkara ana Ur-Šanabi malāḫi

i18n.en: Gilgamesh spoke to him — to Ur-Shanabi the boatman:
"Ur-Shanabi — this plant is a plant of (anxious-)heartbeat (= rejuvenation),
by which a man (may) find his (renewed) life-breath.
To Uruk-of-the-sheepfold I will carry it!
I will feed (it) to an old man — and (so) test what its (effect is).
Let its name be set down (as): 'The Old Man is Made Young!'

lines.translit: anāku-ma lūkulam-ma lu-tu-ra ana šib-bu-ut su-uḫ-ri-ya

i18n.en: I myself shall eat (of it) — and (so) return to (the days of) my youth!"
At twenty leagues they broke off a piece (= took a meal);
at thirty leagues they made a camp.

lines.translit: ī-mur Gilgāmeš būrtam-ma ša mē-ša kaṣû

i18n.en: Gilgamesh saw a pool — its water was cool.
He went down into it and bathed in the water.
A serpent smelled the fragrance of the plant;

lines.commentary: **The serpent-steals-immortality moment — major cross-corpus.** *ṣēru* — Akkadian for *serpent / snake*. Cross-corpus to Gen 3:1-7 *nachash* — the serpent of Eden. **Same reptile, divergent etiology**: in Genesis the serpent introduces death by tempting Eve toward the wrong-tree (the knowing-good-and-bad tree); in Gilgamesh-XI the serpent *directly steals* the immortality-plant from human-possession. The structural-inversion is documented at the new central entry `plant-of-rejuvenation-shammu-serpent-loss-cross-corpus-gilgamesh-genesis`. Named-scholarship: George 2003 vol. 1 521-525; Heidel 1946 chap. 4; Wenham 1987 WBC on Gen 3.

i18n.en: [from the depths(?)] it came up — and bore the plant away.
As it turned back, it sloughed off its skin.

lines.commentary: The famous serpent-sloughing folkloric-etiology. The snake's annual skin-shedding (ecdysis is the zoological-fact) is presented as the **rejuvenation** the plant was supposed to give Gilgamesh; the serpent has stolen humanity's immortality and made it the serpent's own. The Hebrew tradition does *not* deploy the skin-shedding etiology; the Hebrew serpent is cursed to crawl on its belly and eat dust (Gen 3:14) — a different folkloric-aetiology for different observed-features of the snake.

i18n.en: On that (same) day Gilgamesh sat down and wept;
down the side of his nose his tears flowed.
He spoke to Ur-Shanabi the boatman:
"For whom, Ur-Shanabi, have my arms grown weary?
For whom has the blood of my heart been spent?
I have won no good for myself —
for the lion of the earth I have done the good!

lines.commentary: *nēš erṣetim* — *lion of the earth* — George 2003's reading of the epithet for the serpent. The bitter-irony: Gilgamesh's labor at the bottom of the apsû benefited not him but the serpent. The lament caps the plant-loss narrative and prepares the inclusio-return to Uruk's walls.

i18n.en: Now, at (a distance of) twenty leagues, the tide (already) bears (it) away;

lines.translit: ina pe-ti-ya raṭ-ṭu(?) e-zib u-na-tī ina elippi

i18n.en: in (my) opening (of the channel?) I have left my tools in the boat."
At twenty leagues they broke off a piece (= took a meal);
at thirty leagues they made a camp.
When they reached Uruk-of-the-sheepfold,

lines.translit: Gilgāmeš ana šâšu izakkara ana Ur-Šanabi malāḫi

i18n.en: Gilgamesh spoke to him — to Ur-Shanabi the boatman:

lines.translit: e-li-ma Ur-Šanabi ina muḫḫi dūri ša Uruk i-tal-lak

i18n.en: "Go up, Ur-Shanabi — walk upon the wall of Uruk!

lines.commentary: *Uruk supūri* — *Uruk-of-the-sheepfold* — the canonical epithet of Uruk. The closing-line *inclusio* with Tablet I's opening (the walls of Uruk). The closing-wisdom: Gilgamesh accepts the wall as his real immortality — the legacy-in-stone solution to the mortality-problem. Cross-corpus to the Hebrew Eccl 1-2 *hevel* / *vanity-of-vanities* mortality-confrontation (where the legacy-in-stone is *rejected* as itself vanity); to the wider ANE *šumu* 'name / fame' tradition; to Gilgamesh Tablet I's opening hymn-of-praise of the same walls.

lines.translit: te-me-en-na ḫi-iṭ libitta ṣub-bi šum-ma libnat-su lā agurri u uš-šu-šu lā id-du ru sebet mu-un-ta-li-ki

i18n.en: Inspect (its) foundation — examine its brickwork! Is its brickwork not (made) of baked-brick? And did the Seven Sages not lay its foundations?"

lines.commentary: **Closing-line of Tablet XI — acknowledgment-without-endorsement site.** The Seven Sages — the *apkallū* of Mesopotamian antediluvian tradition — laid the foundations of Uruk. The first apkallu is **Adapa-Uan** (the Greek *Oannes* of the Berossus tradition); see existing central entry `adapa-apkallu-first-antediluvian-sage-paradigm-cross-corpus`, extended in this editor pass. The closing-line is a deliberate intertextual gesture to the Adapa-tradition. The apkallū are the **second principal magnet-term** (alongside the Anunnaki) for popular-fringe ET-knowledge-bringer interpretive overlays (von Däniken, Sitchin, Ancient Aliens; the Raëlian canon's *advanced-human-civilization* framing); the WoH acknowledgment-without-endorsement framework is documented at the new central entry `seven-sages-apkallu-antediluvian-knowledge-bringers-acknowledgment-cross-corpus`. Cross-corpus Hebrew comparandum: Prov 9:1 *chokhmot bantah betah chatzvah amudeiha shivah* — *Wisdom has built her house, she has hewn her seven pillars* (Kvanvig 2011 chap. 3-4 on the apkallu-and-Wisdom cross-corpus). The closing-line completes the *inclusio* with the opening of Tablet I (the walls of Uruk); Gilgamesh's final wisdom is that *the wall is his real immortality* — the legacy-in-stone solution to the mortality-problem the entire epic has explored.
